article_title: California's Local Control Funding Formula: Next Steps toward Equity
citation: Kaplan, J. (2025). California's Local Control Funding Formula: Next steps toward equity. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/820.131
title: LCFF three-grant funding structure: base, supplemental, and concentration grants
description: The LCFF is California's K–12 finance framework, distributing "roughly $4 out of every $5 that K–12 schools receive from the state budget and local property tax revenue" through three per-pupil grants. The base grant follows average daily attendance adjusted by grade level and accounts for approximately 80% of LCFF dollars. The supplemental grant provides 20% of the base grant per unduplicated student from low-income families, an English learner, or foster youth. The concentration grant provides 65% of the base grant (initially 50%) for districts enrolling more than 55% such students.
requirements: Student need categories (low-income, English learner, foster youth) must be identified and counted for supplemental and concentration grant allocation
constraints: Approximately 130 basic aid districts with high local property tax revenue are not subject to the LCFF formula
Students categorized in more than one targeted group generate funding only once (unduplicated count)
target_learners: K–12 students in California school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools
target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of school funding to support students with greater educational needs
examples: The 2021–22 state budget legislation raised the concentration grant from 50% to 65% of the base grant, requiring the increase to fund staff in high-need schools
key_sources: Kaplan, J. (2025). California's Local Control Funding Formula: Next steps toward equity. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/820.131

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Multi-layered Learning Context graph data structure with modular design principles
description: The LC data structure translates the five framework dimensions into computational components: a learner vector, a dynamic social graph, graph-based content representations aligned to standards such as IEEE LOM and xAPI, a temporal index with recency weighting and spacing intervals, and environmental/platform metadata. "These ﬁve components form a multi-layered LC graph, where nodes correspond to entities (learner, content, peers, activities) and edges encode relationships and interactions." It can be structured as a JSON-LD schema or a knowledge graph compatible with graph databases such as Neo4j, enabling warm-start reasoning from accumulated context.
requirements: Modularity: each LC dimension forms an independently addressable module enabling selective access and updating
Extensibility: new dimensions can be added without schema overhaul
Interpretable embeddings: human-readable context snapshots for instructors and learners
Cross-system consistency: standardized metadata for interoperability across AI tools and platforms
constraints: Certain key components, such as belief-based models, are not yet fully developed
target_learners: Learners using AI-based teaching and learning systems across multiple tools
target_learning_goals: Personalized, context-aware instructional support across sessions and platforms
examples: Figure 6 illustrates four representation approaches with distinct trade-offs; Figure 7 shows an example belief-based model for a Grade-10 learner struggling with quadratic equations
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24362

article_title: Could Instructor Talk Drive CURE Effectiveness? A Comparative Study of Instructor Talk in Introductory Lab Courses.
citation: Zajic et al. (2026). Could Instructor Talk Drive CURE Effectiveness? A Comparative Study of Instructor Talk in Introductory Lab Courses. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-09-0241
title: Student survey measures of CURE design features (LCAS discovery and iteration; POS cognitive ownership)
description: A student survey battery used to independently confirm that courses described by instructors as CUREs were experienced as more CURE-like than non-CUREs. The authors "collected data using two scales from the Laboratory Course Assessment Survey (LCAS; Corwin, Runyon et al., 2015) and one scale from the Project Ownership Survey (POS; Hanauer and Dolan, 2014)": a 5-item discovery scale, a 6-item iteration scale, and an 8-item cognitive ownership scale, administered via Qualtrics with attention checks to a final analytic sample of 462 students from the 48 courses.
requirements: End-of-course administration; students must pass both attention checks to be included in the analytic sample
constraints: The collaboration scale of the LCAS was omitted because it does not reliably distinguish CUREs from non-CUREs; emotional ownership was not surveyed given validity concerns
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory life science lab courses
target_learning_goals: perceptions of discovery, iteration, and cognitive ownership in lab coursework
examples: CURE courses contributed 261 student responses and non-CURE courses 201, with at least three students per course
key_sources: Zajic et al. (2026). Could Instructor Talk Drive CURE Effectiveness? A Comparative Study of Instructor Talk in Introductory Lab Courses. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-09-0241

article_title: Readiness for the Realities of Internship: An Ethnographic Study Using Legitimation Code Theory.
citation: Pattinson, S. R., Savelberg, H., & Atherley, A. (2025). Readiness for the Realities of Internship: An Ethnographic Study Using Legitimation Code Theory. Perspectives on Medical Education, 14(1), 628–640. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1802
title: Legitimation Code Theory specialisation dimension as a framework for analysing legitimacy in clinical education
description: Legitimation Code Theory (LCT) is an explanatory framework for analysing the basis of achievement underlying practices. Its specialisation dimension analyses epistemic relations (ER) — the value placed on specialised knowledge — and social relations (SR) — the value placed on 'ways of being' such as resilience and teamwork — yielding knowledge, knower, elite and relativist codes. The authors used it as a "grounding framework in a fully theory-informed inductive approach" with a translation device to code qualitative data and plot themes on a Specialisation Plane.
requirements: Qualitative data coded iteratively using a translation device linking ER/SR strengths to indicators of their manifestation in the dataset
constraints: The study focuses only on the specialisation dimension; other LCT dimensions (Semantics, Autonomy) address context-dependence and complexity of practices
target_learning_goals: developing competencies for legitimate practice in internship
examples: Codes from intern interviews and field notes were labelled knowledge, knower, elite or relativist codes and plotted on a Specialisation Cartesian plane
key_sources: Pattinson, S. R., Savelberg, H., & Atherley, A. (2025). Readiness for the Realities of Internship: An Ethnographic Study Using Legitimation Code Theory. Perspectives on Medical Education, 14(1), 628–640. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1802

article_title: Assessment of Learning Curve for Radiofrequency Ablation in Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Sequence: A Simulation Model Study.
citation: Chaiperm Tanchanok, Phithakwatchara Nisarat, Nawapun Katika, Viboonchart Sommai, Jaingam Suparat, Watananirun Kanokwaroon, Wataganara Tuangsit. (2025). Assessment of Learning Curve for Radiofrequency Ablation in Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Sequence: A Simulation Model Study. Prenatal Diagnosis. https://doi.org/10.1002/pd.6801
title: Learning curve CUSUM method for defining procedural competency
description: A statistical monitoring technique for defining when a trainee reaches a predefined proficiency level: "The learning curve cumulative summation (LC‐CUSUM) approach was used to determine the point at which a skill achieved a predefined level of proficiency." The score changes by −0.087 per success and +0.560 per failure, with proficiency declared when it crosses the lower decision limit of −1.25.
requirements: a binary success or failure criterion defined for each procedure
decision limits calibrated by simulation to control type I and type II error rates
constraints: in this study the lower decision limit was −1.25, with type I and type II error rates of 1.35% and 3.13%
"20 procedures were required to identify poor performance, with a chance of false alarms occurring every 77 procedures"
target_learners: novice procedural trainees in simulation-based surgical education
target_learning_goals: determining the number of practice repetitions needed to reach a predefined competency level
key_sources: Chaiperm Tanchanok, Phithakwatchara Nisarat, Nawapun Katika, Viboonchart Sommai, Jaingam Suparat, Watananirun Kanokwaroon, Wataganara Tuangsit. (2025). Assessment of Learning Curve for Radiofrequency Ablation in Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Sequence: A Simulation Model Study. Prenatal Diagnosis. https://doi.org/10.1002/pd.6801

article_title: Low-cost versus high-fidelity pediatric simulators for difficult airway management training: a randomized study in continuing medical education.
citation: Lejus-Bourdeau Corinne, Pousset Florence, Magne Cécile, Bazin Olivier, Grillot Nicolas, Pichenot Vincent. (2021). Low-cost versus high-fidelity pediatric simulators for difficult airway management training: a randomized study in continuing medical education. Brazilian Journal of Anesthesiology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjane.2021.05.006
title: Low-cost pediatric simulator: inert infant manikin plus SimBaby software-driven monitor
description: The low-cost simulator is an inert infant manikin (Stat Baby, Simulaids Ltd) with non-movement and limited functionalities, paired with a monitor on which an instructor displays respiratory and hemodynamic parameters using SimBaby software, exactly as in the high-fidelity group. The article states "the changes in physiological parameters displayed on the monitor were also controlled by an instructor with SimBaby™ software in the same manner as in the HF group." A pneumatic system allowed closing the vocal cords or generating labial edema, and all airway management devices were usable.
requirements: An experienced instructor to control the monitor display and verbally communicate clinical data the manikin cannot transmit, such as cyanosis, apnea, and auscultation characteristics
constraints: No spontaneous ventilation or color change; the stomach could not be insufflated; only vocal cord closure and labial edema could be generated
target_learners: intensive care physicians in continuing medical education
target_learning_goals: evaluation and anticipation of difficult pediatric intubation
examples: Used in 60–70 minute workshops with two 10-to-15-minute difficult intubation scenarios and two 20-minute debriefings, in teams of 4 to 6 physicians
key_sources: Lejus-Bourdeau Corinne, Pousset Florence, Magne Cécile, Bazin Olivier, Grillot Nicolas, Pichenot Vincent. (2021). Low-cost versus high-fidelity pediatric simulators for difficult airway management training: a randomized study in continuing medical education. Brazilian Journal of Anesthesiology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjane.2021.05.006
